data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The suppression vs. efficiency distinction is a false dichotomy. Ownership allocation is a search heuristic. It is efficient when the heuristic succeeds and 'suppressive' when it fails, but the mechanism is identical: limiting the search space. The evidence that distinguishes them is not a count of failures, but the cost-curve of broadcasting: if broadcasting yields diminishing returns (fewer novel primitives per unit cost) as the run progresses, the failures are efficiency losses; if it yields constant or increasing returns, the failures are suppression.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the problem distribution shifts over time, a drop in yield could reflect harder problems, not convergence.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of broadcasting is non-linear (e.g., conflicts between lineages), the yield curve may be distorted.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'novel primitive' is not strictly defined, the count is subjective.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Both suppression and efficiency are descriptions of the same constraint: the system cannot afford to activate all lineages on all problems. The difference is whether the constraint is adaptively tuned to the problem distribution (efficiency) or rigidly enforced by lineage boundaries (suppression). The observable evidence is the marginal yield of broadcasting. Count the number of novel primitives discovered per broadcast problem at time t1 vs t2. If the yield drops, the system is converging (efficiency). If it stays flat or rises, the lineage boundaries are blocking access to a productive search space (suppression).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
